questions.text: A resort property is classified under which occupancy group?

options.text: Group C (Education/Recreation), which includes facilities primarily for educational and recreational purposes
Group E (Business/Mercantile), typically for commercial establishments and offices
Group D (Institutional), which covers buildings used for medical care or other institutional purposes

rationale.a: Group C is for education and recreation facilities like schools and churches, not overnight accommodations.
rationale.c: ERR-DSGN-001: Group E is mercantile/business (offices, retail). Hotels are NOT Group E despite having restaurants.
rationale.d: Group D is institutional (hospitals, jails). Resorts do not provide custodial care.
rationale.correct: Group B is the correct classification for hotels, dormitories, pensions, and resorts per PD 1096. Overnight occupancy use defines Group B.
rationale.takeaway: Resort classification is Group B regardless of amenities; distinguish from Group E even if dining is present.

questions.text: An unsprinklered resort assembly area has an occupant load of 150 persons. According to PD 1096 Section 906, what is the maximum travel distance to the nearest exit?

rationale.a: 30 m is too restrictive and not a standard code limit.
rationale.c: 60 m applies only to sprinklered buildings, not unsprinklered.
rationale.correct: Unsprinklered buildings allow 45 m maximum travel distance per RA 9514 2019 IRR Section 10.2.5.2.7. Sprinklered buildings allow 60 m.
rationale.takeaway: Unsprinklered = 45 m; sprinklered = 60 m travel distance. This is a critical fire safety baseline.

questions.text: A beach resort has indoor assembly areas and an outdoor pavilion (assembly). The outdoor pavilion is unsprinklered and must serve 80 occupants. According to PD 1096 Section 906, how many exits are required?

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-021: Single exit allowed only up to 49 persons. 80 occupants require minimum 2 exits.
rationale.c: Three exits not required unless occupancy exceeds special assembly thresholds (typically 200+ for large venues).
rationale.d: Four exits exceed the minimum requirement for 80 occupants.
rationale.correct: RA 9514 2019 IRR Section 10.2.5.1 requires 2 exits when occupant load ≥50 persons. At 80 occupants, 2 exits minimum required.
rationale.takeaway: Occupancy threshold = 50 persons. Below 50 = 1 exit allowed. At 50+ = 2 exits minimum.

questions.text: An eco-tourism resort has a main dining hall with 300-person capacity. What is the minimum required exit width if the hall is unsprinklered?

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-019: Using 5 mm/person is substandard and fails fire safety requirements.
rationale.c: 10 mm/person exceeds code requirements; 7.6 mm is the standard.
rationale.d: 900 mm is the accessible door width minimum, not an exit calculation for large occupancies.
rationale.correct: Exit width = occupancy × 7.6 mm/person per RA 9514 2019 IRR Section 10.2.5.2. 300 × 7.6 = 2280 mm (2.28 m).
rationale.takeaway: Exit width formula: occupants × 7.6 mm/person. For 300 people, minimum 2280 mm required.

questions.text: An eco-resort proposal includes a mix of Group B (guest rooms) and Group E (main restaurant) functions within one complex. How should the occupancy classification be determined?

options.text: Classify entire complex as Group E due to prominent dining, ensuring compliance with all relevant health and safety regulations for food service establishments
Classify entire complex as Group B if overnight accommodation is primary use; evaluate restaurant separately for fire safety.
Use average occupancy group (midpoint between B and E), which may require additional safety measures to accommodate mixed-use requirements
Classify as Group H (Assembly) because multiple use types exist, necessitating a comprehensive review of all applicable building codes

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-001: Presence of restaurant does NOT reclassify resort to Group E. Primary use (lodging) determines classification.
rationale.c: No intermediate group classification exists. Use primary occupancy category.
rationale.d: Group H (Assembly) applies to sports venues, concert halls with large standing occupancies—not mixed-use resorts.
rationale.correct: Mixed-use complexes are classified by PRIMARY occupancy. If overnight lodging is principal use, classify as Group B. Restaurant (Group E) is evaluated separately for egress, parking, and FSDO compliance.
rationale.takeaway: Mixed-use: Classify by PRIMARY occupancy. Resort (lodging primary) = Group B. Restaurant evaluated separately for code compliance.

questions.text: According to PD 1096 2004 IRR Rule XIX, how many parking spaces must a luxury resort with 200 guest rooms provide?

rationale.a: 50 spaces is insufficient; this would only satisfy first-class hotel ratios (1/2 rooms) at incorrect scale.
rationale.b: 100 spaces applies to first-class hotels at 1:2 ratio, not de luxe properties.
rationale.d: 150 spaces is an incorrect intermediate calculation not referenced in code.
rationale.correct: De luxe hotels require 1 parking space per 2 rooms per PD 1096 2004 IRR Rule XIX. 200 rooms = 100 spaces minimum.
rationale.takeaway: De luxe = 1/room; first-class = 1/2 rooms. Always apply the higher standard for luxury properties.

questions.text: A mountain eco-resort requires accessible parking. According to BP 344, what are the dimensions of a single accessible parking stall?

rationale.a: 3.6 m width × 5.0 m depth exceeds requirements; 2.4 m × 5.0 m is the standard (non-accessible) parking stall dimension.
rationale.b: 3.0 m × 5.5 m is incorrect; accessible width must be 4.0 m.
rationale.correct: BP 344 specifies accessible parking stalls at 4.0 m width × 5.0 m depth to accommodate wheelchair access lanes.
rationale.takeaway: Standard stall = 2.5 × 5.0 m. Accessible stall = 4.0 × 5.0 m. Remember the wider requirement for ADA compliance.

questions.text: A resort design requires an accessible guest room entrance. According to BP 344, what is the minimum door width for accessible entry?

rationale.a: 750 mm is substandard and creates barrier for wheelchair accessibility.
rationale.b: ERR-DSGN-015: 800 mm is insufficient; accessibility standard is 900 mm minimum.
rationale.d: 1000 mm exceeds code; 900 mm is the required minimum.
rationale.correct: BP 344 2024 IRR §302 requires accessible door openings of minimum 900 mm width to accommodate wheelchairs.
rationale.takeaway: Accessible door minimum = 900 mm. Common error is designing at 800 mm.

questions.text: A resort architect must decide between an unsprinklered design (45 m travel distance) and a sprinklered design (60 m travel distance) for a central guest corridor. Which approach provides greater design flexibility, and why?

options.text: Unsprinklered provides more flexibility due to shorter distance, reducing exit count, which can be advantageous in certain layouts
Sprinklered provides more flexibility; longer travel distance (60 m vs. 45 m) allows fewer exits and longer corridors.
Both options provide equal flexibility because exit width calculations compensate for distance differences, balancing design choices
Neither provides flexibility; code requires exits every 30 m regardless of sprinkler status, which limits design options

rationale.a: Unsprinklered is MORE restrictive (45 m limit), reducing flexibility and requiring more exits.
rationale.c: Travel distance and exit width are separate calculations. Distance directly affects exit location frequency.
rationale.d: 30 m is not a code threshold. The limits are 45 m (unsprinklered) and 60 m (sprinklered).
rationale.correct: Sprinklered buildings allow 60 m travel distance vs. 45 m for unsprinklered (per PD 1096 §906). This permits longer corridors and potentially fewer exits, increasing design flexibility and guest room yield.
rationale.takeaway: Sprinkler installation extends allowable travel distance from 45 m to 60 m, enabling more efficient corridor layouts.

questions.text: A resort corridor connecting guest rooms has a required ramp section due to site grade changes. According to BP 344, what is the maximum ramp slope permitted?

rationale.a: ERR-DSGN-014: 1:10 slope is steeper than code allows and creates accessibility barriers.
rationale.c: 1:8 slope is far too steep and violates accessibility requirements.
rationale.d: 1:15 is steeper than needed but more restrictive than code; 1:12 is the standard.
rationale.correct: BP 344 2024 IRR §206 specifies maximum ramp slope of 1:12 (8.3% grade) for accessibility compliance.
rationale.takeaway: Maximum ramp slope = 1:12. Steeper slopes (1:10, 1:8) fail accessibility requirements.
